transcription.text: At the West Coast Computer Fair in 1981, when we introduced the oscilloscope, it's in there,
behind plexiglass, being admired by people, but you can't use it yet.
A guy came over to me and he had a, he said, let me show you something. And he gave me an
Aztec switching power supply and said, this can do the following. And I knew we use those and we
have a problem with heat, a problem with weight, problem with size. This is our solution. He was
the sales representative from Aztec at the right place at the right time.
And so right away, you know, there's a, the first prototypes have spaces for power regulators,
and then it would make a lot of heat. Those disappeared. And of course, the board was
relayed out. It all worked adequately. And one thing Adam said was,
adequacy is sufficient. Nothing, everything else is irrelevant.
In the early computer industry, adequate was sufficient.
And at the trade shows, I would get a few drinks under my belt and start proclaiming,
Osborne Computer, setting new standards in adequacy.
